title: Myth: Hinduism is Polytheistic
short: Reality: One Supreme Reality (Brahman) expressed in many forms.
description: Hinduism ultimately speaks of a single Supreme Reality...
proofs: Rig Veda 1.164.46 – 'Truth is One, sages call it by many names.'

title: Myth: Sati Pratha is Core to Hinduism
short: Reality: Sati was a social evil, not Vedic practice.
description: Sati was never prescribed in Vedas; it emerged in medieval times...
proofs: Rig Veda 10.18.7 encourages widows to return to society, not self-immolate.
Historical evidence shows Sati emerged in medieval India, not in Vedic times.

title: Myth: Idol Worship is Blind Faith
short: Reality: Idols help focus the mind during worship.
description: Idols are symbolic representations that help devotees concentrate and meditate on the divine. They are tools for spiritual focus, not objects of superstition.
proofs: Idol worship is explained as a support for the mind in meditation in Bhagavad Gita 12.2-5.
Ancient temples are designed as symbolic representations of cosmic principles.

title: Myth: Caste System is Core to Hinduism
short: Reality: Original Varna system was based on qualities, not birth.
description: Ancient Hindu texts describe Varna based on one's nature (Guna) and duties (Karma). Discrimination by birth is a later distortion, not part of true Sanatana Dharma.
proofs: Bhagavad Gita 4.13 – Krishna declares that the Varna system is based on Guna (qualities) and Karma (actions).
Birth-based caste discrimination is not supported in core scriptures.

references.text: Rig Veda 10.90.12 - Purusha Sukta describes Varna as cosmic functions, not hierarchy

title: Myth: Hinduism is Only Rituals
short: Reality: Its essence is self-realization and dharma.
description: While rituals exist, Hinduism emphasizes spiritual growth, self-realization, and living in harmony with dharma. Meditation, devotion, and righteous action are central practices.
proofs: Katha Upanishad and Bhagavad Gita emphasize knowledge and self-realization over rituals.
Bhagavad Gita 9.26 teaches devotion and simplicity in worship over ritual complexity.

title: Myth: Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas are the Same
short: Reality: They are different works from different times and languages.
description: Valmiki's Ramayana is the original Sanskrit epic written in ancient times, focusing on Lord Rama's life and dharma. Tulsidas' Ramcharitmanas, written in Awadhi in the 16th century, retells the story with a devotional and poetic emphasis for the common people.
proofs: Valmiki Ramayana has ~24,000 verses in Sanskrit; Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi with ~12,000 verses.
Ramcharitmanas is a Bhakti-era retelling emphasizing devotion.

references.text: Valmiki Ramayana vs Ramcharitmanas - ISKCON Article

title: Myth: Bhagavad Gita and Shrimad Bhagavatam are the Same
short: Reality: They are distinct texts with different focuses.
description: The Bhagavad Gita is a 700-verse dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna in the Mahabharata, focusing on dharma and self-realization. The Shrimad Bhagavatam (Bhagavata Purana) is a devotional text narrating the life and teachings of Lord Krishna and other avatars, emphasizing bhakti (devotion).
proofs: Bhagavad Gita is part of Mahabharata (Bhishma Parva).
Shrimad Bhagavatam is one of the 18 Puranas with 12 cantos.

title: Myth: Men and Women Can Wear Kalawa on Any Wrist
short: Reality: Hindu scriptures clearly prescribe right wrist for men and left wrist for women.
description: The sacred thread (kalawa, mauli, raksha-sutra) is not tied randomly. Hindu scriptures prescribe that men should wear it on the right wrist, while women should wear it on the left wrist. This distinction is rooted in symbolism and ritual science: the right side represents Purusha (masculine, solar, active energy), and the left represents Prakriti (feminine, lunar, nurturing energy). Thus, wearing kalawa on different wrists aligns with cosmic balance and dharmic tradition.
proofs: Bhagavata Purana 8.22–23, Skanda Purana – Lakshmi ties a raksha-sutra to King Bali as Vamana blesses him.
Mahabharata (folk retellings, Vrata Kathas) – Kunti ties a protective thread on Abhimanyu; as long as it remained intact, he was invincible.
Paraskara Grihya Sutra 2.2.4–6 – 'दक्षिणे पुरुषाणां, वामे स्त्रीणाम्' (dakṣiṇe puruṣāṇām, vāme strīṇām) — For men it is on the right, for women on the left.

Āpastamba Grihya Sutra 1.1.1.12 – 'शुभकर्मणि दक्षिणहस्तः, स्त्रीणां वामहस्तः' (śubhakarmaṇi dakṣiṇa-hastaḥ, strīṇāṁ vāma-hastaḥ) — In auspicious rituals, the right hand is prescribed for men, and the left hand for women.

Skanda Purana, Kashi Khanda 16 – 'रक्षासूत्रं पुंसां दक्षिणे, स्त्रीणां वामे विधीयते' (rakṣā-sūtraṁ puṁsāṁ dakṣiṇe, strīṇāṁ vāme vidhīyate) — The protective thread should be tied on the right wrist of men, and on the left wrist of women.

Dharma Sindhu – 'रक्षासूत्रं पुरुषस्य दक्षिणे, स्त्रियाः वामे बन्धनीयम्' (rakṣā-sūtraṁ puruṣasya dakṣiṇe, striyāḥ vāme bandhanīyam) — The raksha-sutra should be tied on the right wrist of a man, and on the left wrist of a woman.

Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva 137 – 'ब्राह्मे मुहूर्ते रक्षां बध्नन्ति मनुजेषु च। दक्षिणे पुरुषाणां तु, स्त्रीणां वामे प्रकीर्तितम्॥' — At the auspicious hour, the raksha is tied to humans too — on the right wrist of men, and on the left of women.

title: Why are Lakshmi and Ganesha Worshipped on Diwali?
short: Lakshmi Ji brings prosperity, while Ganesha Ji ensures wisdom and removes obstacles.
description: On the festival of Diwali, Maa Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and prosperity, is worshipped to invite abundance and fortune into homes. Lord Ganesha, the remover of obstacles and giver of wisdom, is worshipped alongside Lakshmi Ji to ensure that prosperity is attained and used wisely. The combination symbolizes 'Shubh' (auspiciousness) and 'Labh' (benefit), ensuring a balanced and successful life. Spiritually, Diwali night is believed to be the most powerful time to invoke these blessings, as it marks the triumph of light over darkness.
proofs: Lakshmi Puja on Diwali is mentioned in Skanda Purana as a way to invite prosperity.
Lord Ganesha is invoked at the beginning of all auspicious works as per the Ganesha Atharvashirsha.
The pairing of Lakshmi (wealth) and Ganesha (wisdom) is symbolized in 'Shubh-Labh', seen in scriptures and traditional practices.

references.text: Skanda Purana – Lakshmi Puja on Diwali night

title: Myth: Rice in Tika is only for decoration
short: Reality: Rice (Akshata) symbolizes prosperity, wholeness, and divine blessings.
description: Many people think that adding rice to tika is just a decorative ritual. In reality, the use of rice, called 'Akshata' (unbroken grain), carries deep symbolic meaning. Rice represents life, prosperity, and sustenance. Being unbroken, it signifies completeness and undiminished blessings. When applied on the forehead along with kumkum or chandan, it is placed on the Ajna Chakra (third eye) to invoke divine energy, wisdom, and good fortune. Thus, rice in tika is not merely decoration, but a sacred symbol of prosperity and wholeness.
proofs: The Sanskrit term 'Akshata' means unbroken, complete, and undiminished, symbolizing fullness and prosperity.
Forehead application (between eyebrows) aligns with the Ajna Chakra, invoking spiritual energy and divine grace.
Traditional Hindu rituals use rice as an offering to deities, linking it with blessings of health, wealth, and wisdom.

references.text: Significance of Akshata in Hindu rituals

title: Myth: Hinduism has 33 crore (330 million) gods
short: Reality: 'Koti' means 'type/category', not 'crore'—there are 33 principal deities symbolizing aspects of the One Supreme Reality.
description: A common misconception is that Hinduism believes in 33 crore (330 million) gods. In fact, the Vedas and Upanishads mention '33 koti devas,' where 'koti' means 'type' or 'class,' not 'crore.' These 33 categories of deities (12 Adityas, 11 Rudras, 8 Vasus, and 2 Ashvins) represent different manifestations of the One Supreme (Brahman).
proofs: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.9.1 – Enumerates 33 devas: 12 Adityas, 11 Rudras, 8 Vasus, and 2 Ashvins.
Yajurveda 32.1 – Affirms One Supreme Reality (Brahman) from whom all manifestations arise.

title: Myth: Vedas and Puranas are the same
short: Reality: Vedas are Shruti (eternal revelations), while Puranas are Smriti (remembered stories and teachings). They differ in origin, purpose, and style.
description: The Vedas and the Puranas serve different roles in Hindu tradition. The Vedas are the most ancient scriptures, considered Shruti—divine revelations 'heard' by rishis. They focus on hymns, rituals, philosophy, and spiritual truths. The Puranas, on the other hand, are Smriti—texts compiled by sages like Vyasa, presenting mythology, stories of gods and avatars, cosmology, and moral teachings in an accessible way for the masses. Vedas are abstract and philosophical, while Puranas are narrative and devotional.
proofs: Rig Veda – oldest scripture of Hinduism, containing hymns and philosophy.
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad – Vedic philosophy teaching Atman and Brahman.
Bhagavata Purana – narrates stories of Lord Vishnu and his avatars.
Shiva Purana – narrates cosmic stories of Lord Shiva.
